newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Smaller Dutch firms outpace AEX record run.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Smaller Dutch firms outpace AEX record run.

text.p: The Dutch AEX blue-chip index has climbed nearly 30 percent this year but many of the Dutch market's minnows are doing even better, with some top performers adding around 200 percent in value.

Analysts say small firms are benefiting from the surge in world stock markets as Dutch players cast around for investment opportunities, seeking to tap into better returns than the historical average of seven percent or so offered by larger companies.

"Volumes have risen considerably over the past year, there's much stronger demand for the smaller segment of the market. We quite agree with that basically, because we think that is where the potential is," said George Raven, an analyst with Insinger de Beaufort.
"Of course not every year will be as good as the past year but our own portfolio of small and midcap stocks over the past 1-1/2 years has doubled in value," he said.
GOUDSMIT STAR PERFORMER

Analysts point to employment services group Goudsmit as the market's star performer. Goudsmit shares have rocketed 239 percent in the past 12 months to around 154.50 guilders after news of a key divestment and acquisitions.
Not far behind is Computer Management Group whose price has risen some 211 percent since the beginning of the year to a high in November of 25.80 guilders.

But even without the incentive of a boom year and special situations, smaller firms routinely offer value compared to the bigger stocks, reflecting the sector's lack of liquidity and unpredictability.

"We would say a reasonable average return on the large caps would be around seven percent and with a well-focused small cap portfolio you may be able to get a return which is closer to double that," said Raven.
Analysts say investors are drawn to the small cap sector because the businesses tend to be young, growing from a smaller base and thus offering bigger potential yields.
"In years to come companies like Unilever should find it very difficult to raise their prices in an environment where inflation is dormant," said Raven.

"We don't have very high hopes of earnings improvements in companies like that, while smaller companies can have their own niche in a certain market in which they can do very well. Starting from a lower base -- say 10 rather than 10,000 -- it's much easier to realise a 10 percent increase," he added.

Smaller firms also have the inherent advantage of trading at a discount to bigger names, partly because the stocks tend to be infrequently traded and corporate announcements on developments and strategy can be patchy.
"It's interesting to invest in small caps because they are traded at a discount to the total market," said Michael Bosman of ING Barings.

"There's always a discount of around 20 percent to the total market, mainly because small caps are not liquid, investors are unfamiliar with the company and news is only available twice a year when the company reports figures," Bosman said.
"Some small caps are very interesting at the moment because investors are seeing that the (AEX) index is rather high and they're looking at stocks which have a rather low valuation," said Bosman.
LOWER PROFILE IS ATTRACTIVE
The low profile of small firms can actually be what is most attractive about them, with the chance to unearth a gem that has been overlooked by others.
"The advantage is that you discover developments that are not reflected in the share price, sometimes you see really cheap shares," said Rene Verhoef of NIB Strating.

One analyst said he had picked hotel and restaurant group Krasnapolsky NV after it pulled out of its Lido Restaurants unit. "It more than doubled earnings per share after that, which had an enormous impact," he said.

Krasnapolsky shares have risen 126 percent in the past year while 1995 earnings per share of 6.72 guilders are predicted to jump to 13.00 guilders in 1996 and 15.00 guilders in 1997 according to consensus estimates gathered by Reuters.
Verhoef says the time-consuming nature of poring over small company statements, crunching numbers and getting in contact with management can deter some investors.

"You need to invest a lot of time. Most brokers are not interested because they look at the daily turnovers and they're often too small to justify it from a commercial point of view. That's why it's an interesting market and why you can make a higher return than on the bigger stocks," he said.

He said fast-growing profits were not the only sign that investors could be on to a winner. "It varies, but in general the ratio that tends to take my interest first is price below book value and whether it offers an attractive dividend yield. If I see that combination, then I start to look closer at the company."
Analysts say that although they routinely look at investment ratios when picking potential winners, fundamentals -- such as the nature of the management and its strategy -- also play a key role.
"It's riskier than the big caps because you have less information, the positive side is that you can speak much more openly with the management. They are prepared to tell you more," said Verhoef.
But the illiquidity and potential unpredictability of smaller firms are what inject the risk into investing in the sector.
"When there is bad news and you want to sell the stock it's impossible because there is no demand or demand at 10 percent lower," said ING's Bosman.
Analysts say investors who put their money into small firms generally work hard for their higher returns and constitute a breed apart from those who slug it out in the big ones.

"They're the kind who really love equities, because you have to put a lot of effort into it. You must have patience because you can be right but it can take six months before you see any move in the share price," said Verhoef.
"It's much more fun, because you can be rewarded for your ideas, whereas your added value for a big stock is likely to be less."
